record.title: Score distributions improve retrieval abstention on reasoning-heavy tasks
record.summary: The authors evaluate six zero-cost query-performance predictors across 11 retrieval architectures and 28 datasets spanning semantic, logical and temporal tasks. They report that score-distribution signals such as Score Gap and LSMV outperform raw maximum-score confidence on reasoning-intensive retrieval, with AUROC gains up to 0.16 where magnitude-based confidence is weak. The paper’s end-to-end BRIGHT answer-quality test uses one generator and one judge; no independent reproduction or production-distribution validation was conducted.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 11 retrieval architectures and 28 datasets, the authors report that distribution-based predictors outperform raw maximum-score confidence on logical and temporal retrieval; reported AUROC gains reach 0.16 in settings where magnitude is weak.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that Score Gap and a variance-based score signal improve downstream answer quality in an end-to-end BRIGHT test using Qwen3.6-27B as generator and GPT-4o as judge.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports that these predictors use the existing top-k retrieval-score distribution and require no additional model inference or retraining.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction has tested the paper’s retrieval predictor comparisons or downstream answer-quality result. The end-to-end evaluation uses one generator and one judge.
The evaluation uses public BEIR, BRIGHT and TEMPO benchmarks; behavior under proprietary corpora, production query distributions and custom retriever training is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated in deployed RAG systems, stronger zero-cost retrieval abstention could reduce downstream errors without additional inference cost, changing local evaluation and reliability choices. Current evidence is benchmark-bounded and the only end-to-end test uses one generator and judge.
limitations: The end-to-end BRIGHT answer-quality evaluation uses one generator (Qwen3.6-27B) and one judge (GPT-4o); transfer to other architectures and evaluation protocols is untested.
Experiments use public benchmarks and may not match proprietary corpora, production query distributions or custom-trained retrievers.
The paper does not establish an absolute performance ceiling for zero-cost abstention or close the gap to cross-encoder reranking and model-based verification.
Results are author-reported; the research desk did not independently execute the paper’s code or reproduce the measurements.
brief.summary: The authors evaluate six zero-cost query-performance predictors across 11 retrieval architectures and 28 datasets spanning semantic, logical and temporal tasks. They report that score-distribution signals such as Score Gap and LSMV outperform raw maximum-score confidence on reasoning-intensive retrieval, with AUROC gains up to 0.16 where magnitude-based confidence is weak. The paper’s end-to-end BRIGHT answer-quality test uses one generator and one judge; no independent reproduction or production-distribution validation was conducted.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that zero-cost distributional predictors, especially Score Gap and LSMV, improve retrieval-success prediction across semantic, logical and temporal benchmarks; the largest reported AUROC gain is 0.16.
technical.demonstrated_result: No independent result was demonstrated by the research desk. The paper reports up to 0.16 AUROC improvement for distribution-based query-performance predictors over maximum-score confidence in selected settings.
technical.mechanism: Estimate query-level retrieval success from the shape of the top-k retrieval-score distribution (for example, the leading-score gap or score variance) rather than treating the absolute maximum similarity score as calibrated confidence.
technical.regime: Eleven retrieval architectures and 28 datasets across BEIR semantic retrieval, BRIGHT logical reasoning and TEMPO temporal reasoning; top-k retrieval-score statistics. The end-to-end answer-quality experiment is on BRIGHT with Qwen3.6-27B and GPT-4o.
technical.reproducibility: arXiv full text and appendices provide benchmark tables and method descriptions. No independent execution by the research desk; production-corpus transfer and additional generator/judge results remain unavailable.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper’s raw maximum retrieval score (MaxScore) baseline, compared with Score Gap and other distributional metrics using the same ranked retrieval results and benchmark protocol.

brief.title: Score distributions improve retrieval abstention on reasoning-heavy tasks
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported pattern transfers, RAG systems can make more reliable retrieval-abstention decisions from existing scores without extra inference, retraining or latency. The evidence is limited to the paper’s public benchmarks and one end-to-end generator/judge, so it does not establish production-wide gains.
